Chronology 5 — Moses and the Exodus

Moses (Musa) is the most-mentioned figure in the Qur'an; the parallel with the Bible is the closest in the whole storyline — which makes the divergences especially diagnostic.

Shared narrative

Birth under threat and the basket on the river; flight to Midian; the burning bush/fire and commission; the staff-to-serpent and the "white hand" signs; Aaron given as spokesman for the slow-of-speech Moses; confrontation with Pharaoh; plagues; deliverance through the sea and Pharaoh's destruction; revelation at the mountain; the people's rebellion (the calf). The agreement extends even to specific details (the basket, Midian, the staff, Aaron the helper) — the tightest parallel in the storyline.

What is said at the theophany — a revealing divergence

Both record the bush/fire encounter; what God says about Himself differs, and the difference is diagnostic (it is the cap. 09 seam in miniature):

  • Bible: "I AM WHO I AM (ehyeh asher ehyeh)… say YHWH… this is My name forever" (Exod 3:14–15) — self-disclosure as the covenant name, relational and personal.
  • Qurʾan: "Indeed I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me" (Q 20:14; cf. 27:9; 28:30) — self-disclosure as the *declaration of tawḥīd*** and a command to worship.

Same scene, same prophet — but Exodus discloses a name, the Qurʾan discloses a doctrine. This is the nature-of-God contrast (covenantal self-naming vs. transcendent unity-assertion) surfacing at the very first divine speech to Moses.

The key divergences (text)

1. The golden calf — who is guilty?

  • Bible: Aaron himself makes the calf (Exod 32:2–4) — and the Bible does not whitewash it: "the LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him" (Deut 9:20), yet Aaron still becomes high priest. This is the criterion of embarrassment again (cf. cap. 15): an unflattering detail kept about a hero.
  • Qurʾan: the calf is made by al-Sāmirī; Hārūn is explicitly exonerated — he warns the people and is innocent (Q 20:85–94), protecting *prophetic impeccability (ʿiṣma)*.
  • Symmetry note: critics raise an anachronism objection to "al-Sāmirī" (linking it to the post-exilic Samaritans, centuries later) — structurally the same kind of objection as Haman below. Muslim scholars reply that Sāmirī is a personal/tribal name, not the later Samaritans. Like Haman: a real but contested point, recorded as unresolved, and noted on both sides for symmetry.

2. Pharaoh's end

  • Qur'an-only details: Pharaoh's deathbed profession of faith is rejected (Q 10:90–91) and "We will preserve your body as a sign" (Q 10:92). This has no biblical parallel; modern apologetic use of Egyptian mummies is rhetoric, not proof (Methodology §1.4).

3. The "Haman" question

  • The Qurʾan places a Hāmān in Pharaoh's Egypt as his minister, ordered to build a tower (Q 28:6, 38; 40:36–37).
  • The only biblical Haman is a Persian official in Esther, ~a millennium later and a different empire — the standard anachronism objection.
  • Muslim responses (stated fully): "Hāmān" may be a common name or a title/office; some apologists link it to the Egyptian priestly designation ḥm-nṯr ("servant of the god") — though that etymology is itself rejected by most Egyptologists and should not be oversold.
  • Verdict on this point: the prima facie reading favours the anachronism charge, but it is not a knockout (Methodology §4); paired with the symmetric al-Sāmirī objection, the honest record is contested, not decisive on either side.

4. Dramatic elements unique to each

  • Qurʾan-only: the magicians believe and are martyred by Pharaoh ("we will not prefer you over the clear proofs", Q 20:70–73; 7:120–126) — a vivid faith-under-persecution motif; in the Bible the magicians merely fail and concede "this is the finger of God" (Exod 8:19). Qārūn (Korah), swallowed with his wealth, is moralised as the archetype of arrogant riches (Q 28:76–82).
  • These are theological dramatisations, not corruption proofs — each text shaping the shared events to its own emphasis.

Arbiter verdict — Moses

Present. The richest shared narrative in the storyline; divergences concentrated on moral roles and a few Qur'an-only specifics.

Weigh.

  • Systematic, theology-driven: Aaron's exoneration is internally consistent with ʿiṣma — a doctrine, not a copying slip; the Bible's retention of Aaron's guilt is the criterion of embarrassment.
  • Self-disclosure divergence: "I AM / YHWH" (a name) vs. "I am Allah, no deity but Me" (a doctrine) — the cap. 09 seam, textual and clean.
  • Symmetric contested objections: Hāmān (anachronism vs. Egypt) and al-Sāmirī (anachronism vs. the Samaritans) are the same kind of objection — each prima facie favours the critic, each has a non-trivial rebuttal, neither is decisive. They offset.
  • Out of remit: mummy/concordist arguments and the ḥm-nṯr etymology — rhetoric/disputed, set aside. The external historicity of a large Exodus (debated by archaeologists) pressures both texts equally.

Judge. On the shared core: the strongest draw in the whole storyline — agreement down to specifics. On theophany self- disclosure: a clean divergence tracking cap. 09 (name vs. doctrine), non-arbitrable as to which is "right." On the calf: a doctrine- driven divergence (ʿiṣma vs. embarrassment), each internally coherent. On Hāmān / al-Sāmirī: mutually contested and offsetting — the dossier scores neither as a win (Methodology §4). The seam reappears exactly where Islamic prophetology requires sinless prophets — setting up the next chapter.
